parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem: A source oscillates with frequency $f$ to produce a progressive wave of wavelength $\lambda$. The source takes time $t$ to produce $n$ complete oscillations.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by a progressive wave.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a travelling disturbance actually carries along with it - the particles of the medium only oscillate in place, so what is it that moves forward?
parts.proper_answer: A progressive wave is a wave that transfers / propagates energy from one place to another.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Makes It Progressive**
Imagine flicking one end of a rope. The hump travels along, but each bit of rope just moves up and down and stays where it was. That travelling hump is a progressive wave. It is different from a stationary wave where energy is trapped between nodes.

Step 2: **The Key Definition**
So the essential idea is movement of energy. The particles oscillate but do not travel with the wave. The energy does: $$ \text{progressive wave transfers energy from source outward} $$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
State expressions, in terms of some or all of $f$, $\lambda$ and $n$, for:

- the distance moved by a wavefront in time $t$
- time $t$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus first on distance - if one complete oscillation of the source launches one full wavelength into space, how far will $n$ oscillations have launched in time $t$?
Hint 2: Now focus on time - recall what frequency $f$ means as number of oscillations per unit time, and rearrange it to make time $t$ the subject for $n$ oscillations.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Distance Moved By The Wavefront**
Each time the source does one full oscillation it creates one full wavelength $\lambda$ of wave. After $n$ oscillations, $n$ wavelengths have been laid out behind the leading wavefront. So: $$ \text{distance} = n\lambda $$

Step 2: **Time Taken For n Oscillations**
Frequency is defined as oscillations per second: $$ f = \frac{n}{t} $$ Rearranging for time gives the time to make $n$ oscillations: $$ t = \frac{n}{f} $$

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Use your answers in (ii) to determine an expression for the speed $v$ of the wave in terms of $f$ and $\lambda$.

markscheme_points.text: (v = distance / time) (v) = nλ / (n / f) so (v) = fλ

hints: Hint 1: Think of the most basic definition of speed - total distance divided by total time - and consider substituting your two expressions from (ii) into it and cancelling $n$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Speed = Distance / Time**
Wave speed is just how fast the wavefront moves: $$ v = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} $$ Put in your answers from (ii): $$ v = \frac{n\lambda}{n/f} $$

Step 2: **Cancel To Get The Famous Equation**
The $n$ on top and bottom cancel: $$ v = \frac{n\lambda \times f}{n} = f\lambda $$ This is the universal wave equation, true for all progressive waves.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Two identical microwave sources X and Y emit waves in phase. The sources are separated by a distance of $30\text{ cm}$, as shown in Fig. 4.1.
{{figure:figure_4_1}}
Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)
The intensity of the microwaves is to be investigated at points P and Q. Line PQ is parallel to line XY. Distance XP is equal to distance YP. Distance YQ is $72\text{ cm}$ and angle XYQ is $90^{\circ}$. The wavelength of the microwaves is $4.0\text{ cm}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the frequency, in GHz, of the microwaves.
hints: Hint 1: Microwaves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum, so what speed do they all travel at in air, and how will you express the 4.0 cm wavelength in SI base units of metres before using $v = f\lambda$?
Hint 2: After you find $f$ in Hz, remember $1 \text{ GHz} = 10^9 \text{ Hz}$ - how many powers of ten do you need to divide by?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Up With Correct Units**
All EM waves travel at $c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Convert wavelength: $$ \lambda = 4.0 \text{ cm} = 4.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 0.040 \text{ m} $$ From $v = f\lambda$: $$ f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{4.0 \times 10^{-2}} $$

Step 2: **Calculate And Convert To GHz**
$$ f = 7.5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz} $$ Since $1 \text{ GHz} = 10^9 \text{ Hz}$: $$ f = \frac{7.5 \times 10^9}{10^9} = 7.5 \text{ GHz} $$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the difference between the path lengths XQ and YQ is $6\text{ cm}$.

markscheme_points.text: Or calculate angle Q using tan and then cos to obtain XQ of 78 tan θ = 30 / 72 so θ = 22.6 XQ = 72 / cos 22.6 = 78 (cm) path difference 78 – 72 = 6 (cm)
Or calculate angle X using tan and then cos to obtain XQ of 78 tan θ = 72 / 30 so θ = 67.4 XQ = 72 / sin 67.4 = 78 (cm) path difference 78 – 72 = 6 (cm)

hints: Hint 1: Look at triangle XYQ in Fig. 4.1 - it is right-angled at Y with sides 30 cm and 72 cm, so which side is XQ and which theorem links it to YQ?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find XQ With Pythagoras**
Triangle XYQ is right-angled at Y. XQ is the hypotenuse: $$ XQ = \sqrt{YQ^2 + XY^2} = \sqrt{72^2 + 30^2} $$ $$ XQ = \sqrt{5184 + 900} = \sqrt{6084} = 78 \text{ cm} $$

Step 2: **Subtract To Get Path Difference**
The wave from Y travels $YQ = 72 \text{ cm}$, the wave from X travels $78 \text{ cm}$: $$ \text{path difference} = XQ - YQ = 78 - 72 = 6 \text{ cm} $$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: State and explain what may be deduced about the intensity of the microwaves at point Q.
hints: Hint 1: Start by comparing your 6 cm path difference to the 4.0 cm wavelength - how many wavelengths fit into the extra distance travelled by the X wave?
Hint 2: Recall how path difference in wavelengths converts to phase difference, where one full wavelength equals $360^{\circ}$ - what does a half-integer number of wavelengths imply?
Hint 3: Think about what happens when two identical in-phase sources arrive in antiphase - do the displacements add up or cancel, and what does that mean for intensity?
parts.proper_answer: Path difference $= 6/4 \lambda = 1.5\lambda$. Phase difference $= 1.5 \times 360^{\circ} = 540^{\circ} \equiv 180^{\circ}$, so waves arrive in antiphase and interfere destructively giving minimum intensity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Express Path Difference In Wavelengths**
$$ \text{path difference} = \frac{6.0 \text{ cm}}{4.0 \text{ cm}} = 1.5\lambda $$ A whole number would mean in step, a half-integer means out of step.

Step 2: **Convert To Phase Difference**
One wavelength corresponds to $360^{\circ}$ of phase: $$ \text{phase difference} = 1.5 \times 360^{\circ} = 540^{\circ} $$ Subtracting a full cycle $360^{\circ}$ leaves $180^{\circ}$. The two waves arrive in antiphase.

Step 3: **Deduce Intensity**
In antiphase, crest meets trough and displacements cancel. Since the sources are identical and in phase to start with, this is destructive interference, so the resultant amplitude is minimum and intensity is minimum.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text:
A microwave detector is positioned at P and connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO). The controls of the CRO are adjusted so that a waveform is shown on the screen.

Describe the changes to the amplitude of the waveform as the detector is moved from P to Q.

markscheme_points.text: amplitude changes from maximum (at P) to minimum (at Q)
amplitude changes from maximum (at P) to minimum to maximum to minimum (at Q)

hints: Hint 1: Start at P where XP = YP so the path difference is zero - what type of interference and what amplitude does that give, and what did you just find at Q?
Hint 2: As you slide from P down to Q the path difference grows smoothly from zero to 6 cm (1.5 wavelengths) - how many times will it pass through whole and half-integer wavelengths on the way?
parts.proper_answer: At P path difference is zero so amplitude is maximum. Moving to Q amplitude falls to minimum, rises to maximum, then falls to minimum at Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify The End Points**
At P, $XP = YP$ so path difference is zero. Identical in-phase sources give constructive interference, so CRO amplitude is maximum. At Q you proved destructive interference, so amplitude is minimum.

Step 2: **Track The Pattern Between**
Moving from P to Q the path difference increases steadily from $0$ to $1.5\lambda$. It passes through $0.5\lambda$ (minimum), $1.0\lambda$ (maximum), then $1.5\lambda$ (minimum). So the CRO amplitude goes: maximum to minimum to maximum to minimum.
